text_blocks.snippet: Soft tissue calcification treatment varies depending on the location and severity of the calcium deposits. Treatment can range from conservative approaches like medication and physical therapy to more invasive procedures like steroid injections or even surgery.
snippet_highlighted_words: conservative approaches like medication and physical therapy to more invasive procedures like steroid injections or even surgery

list.snippet: Medications: Over-the-counter NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) can help reduce pain and inflammation associated with calcifications.
Physical Therapy: Exercises to strengthen muscles and improve range of motion can be beneficial, especially for calcifications in tendons.
Heat and/or Ice: Applying heat or ice can help manage pain and inflammation.

list.title: Steroid Injections:
list.snippet: Corticosteroid injections can reduce inflammation and pain, especially in cases of calcific tendonitis.

list.title: Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy (ESWT):
list.snippet: This therapy uses shock waves to break down calcium deposits.

list.title: Percutaneous Needling:
list.snippet: A needle is used to aspirate or break up the calcium deposit under ultrasound guidance.

list.title: Surgical Removal:
list.snippet: In severe cases where conservative treatments fail, surgery may be necessary to remove the calcified tissue.

list.title: Calcific periarthritis:
list.snippet: This condition, which can affect joints and tendons, often resolves on its own, but treatment may be needed for pain and inflammation.

list.title: Calcific myonecrosis:
list.snippet: This rare condition, where muscle tissue hardens due to poor blood flow, may require surgical removal of the calcified tissue and wound reconstruction.

list.title: Hyperphosphatemic Familial Tumoral Calcinosis (HFTC):
list.snippet: In this rare genetic disorder, deep soft-tissue calcifications may require a combination of topical sodium thiosulfate and acetazolamide, along with phosphate-lowering agents.
